questions.solution: 5! (5 factorial) is calculated by multiplying all positive integers from 1 to 5. So, 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.
questions.explanation: Factorial calculations involve multiplying a number by all the numbers below it down to 1.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget to include one or more of the numbers in the multiplication, leading to an incorrect result. For example, choosing A (10) would be a mistake because it only includes two factors (5 and 4), not all five.

questions.solution: 3! (3 factorial) is calculated by multiplying all positive integers from 1 to 3. So, 3! = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.
questions.explanation: Remember that factorial calculations start with 1 and multiply up to the given number.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to include numbers larger than the given one, like choosing C (18) which includes 4 and 5 in the multiplication, which are not part of 3!.

questions.solution: 7! (7 factorial) is calculated by multiplying all positive integers from 1 to 7. So, 7! = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5040.
questions.explanation: Factorial calculations involve multiplying a number by all the numbers below it down to 1.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to forget one of the factors, like choosing B (42) which is missing the factor of 7.

questions.solution: 0! (0 factorial) is defined as 1, according to the convention in mathematics.
questions.explanation: The factorial of 0 is a special case and is set to 1 by definition.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to assume that 0! is 0 or undefined because it doesn't follow the typical pattern of multiplying numbers. However, this is an exception in the factorial function.

questions.solution: 2! (2 factorial) is calculated by multiplying all positive integers from 1 to 2. So, 2! = 2 × 1 = 2.

questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to forget one of the factors, like choosing A (1) which is missing the factor of 2.
